title: Why LLM evaluation is different
summary: Classic tests assert one exact output. LLM features vary run to run, accept many valid answers and fail in stacked layers, so evaluation becomes measurement: a dataset, a scorer with known error, repeated trials and a decision rule.
useIf: You are about to ship or change an LLM feature and must decide how you will know it works.
avoidIf: The output is fully mechanical (a schema, a lookup, a regex) and a plain unit test already covers it.

explain.md: A classic test asserts that one input gives one exact output. An LLM feature breaks that contract in three ways, and each break changes how you measure.

items: **The output varies.** Sampling makes two runs differ. Lowering `temperature` narrows the spread but does not remove it, so one run is a sample, not a fact.

**Many outputs are valid.** An exact match fails a correct answer phrased differently. You need a scorer: code for what can be checked mechanically, a judge model for meaning and tone, a human for taste. Anthropic names these three grader types: code-based, model-based and human [[r17]].
**Failures stack in layers.** A wrong answer can come from retrieval, the prompt, the model, a tool call or the orchestration. One end-to-end score cannot say which.

explain.md: So evaluation is measurement. You need a dataset, a scorer whose error you have measured, enough repeated trials to see past noise, and a decision rule. Quality is also several numbers at once: correctness, groundedness, safety, latency and cost.

explain.title: The measurement loop
explain.alt: A dataset is run through the system several times, scored by code, judge or human, aggregated with an interval, and a decision rule chooses to ship or to fix and add cases.
explain.src:
flowchart LR
  D[Dataset] --> R[Run n trials]
  R --> S[Score: code, judge, human]
  S --> A[Aggregate with interval]
  A --> X{Decision rule}
  X -->|ship| P[Release]
  X -->|fix| D

explain.md: Set the pass bar as a product decision. Hamel Husain notes that, unlike unit tests, you do not need a 100% pass rate: it depends on the failures you are willing to tolerate [[tr6]]. Anthropic separates capability evals, which start at a low pass rate, from regression evals, which should sit near 100% and protect what already works [[r17]].

explain.title: One-line answer
explain.md: LLM evals differ because the system is stochastic, the answer space is open and the faults are layered. So you score by layer, repeat trials and report an interval.

whereToUse: Before the first release of any LLM feature, to get a baseline
On every prompt, model, retriever or tool change as a regression check
When a vendor retires or updates a model version and you must prove parity
When product, risk and engineering disagree and need a shared number

use: The output is free text, a ranking, a plan or a tool sequence
Several components can each cause a bad answer
A wrong answer has a cost you can name
You will change the system repeatedly
avoid: The result is fully checkable by code and a unit test already exists
The feature is a throwaway demo that no one will rely on
A fixed, enumerable input set already has exact expected outputs that code can compare
flips: Harm per wrong answer rises: add safety evaluators, red teaming and human review before launch
A reference answer exists for every case: prefer code checks over a judge
Traffic is large and labels are scarce: lean on online scoring of sampled traces

pitfalls.symptom: The score rose 0.2 but users still complain
pitfalls.cause: The metric does not measure the failing behaviour, or an uncalibrated judge is scoring it
pitfalls.fix: Start from real failure cases, pick a scorer per failure and check judge agreement with a human sample

pitfalls.symptom: The same commit passes on Monday and fails on Tuesday
pitfalls.cause: A single run of a stochastic system, compared with a fixed threshold
pitfalls.fix: Repeat trials, report an interval and compare paired against a baseline

pitfalls.symptom: One blended quality score hides a safety regression
pitfalls.cause: Dimensions were averaged into a single number
pitfalls.fix: Gate each dimension separately and block on safety on its own

scenarios.title: Two-person prototype, no traffic
scenarios.situation: A two-person team has a working assistant that drafts support replies. A human reviews and sends every reply. There is no production traffic, and one domain expert can give two hours a week.
constraints: Expert time is the scarce resource
A human sends every reply, so errors are reversible
unknowns: How many real failure examples already exist?
Can the reviewers' edits be logged?
What would a wrong reply cost the customer?
scenarios.question: How do you start measuring?

options.name: 20 to 50 cases from real failures, code checks plus a pass/fail judge
options.why: It matches the expert budget and gives a regression baseline from day one. Anthropic calls 20 to 50 tasks drawn from real failures a great start [[r17]].
options.tradeoff: A small set cannot see small changes, and the judge needs calibrating against the expert.

options.name: Ship with human review and log the edits as the signal
options.why: Risk is low and reversible, and every edit is a free label.
options.tradeoff: There is no pre-release gate, so regressions appear after users meet them.

options.name: Track a public benchmark score
options.why: It measures other tasks on other data and may be saturated or leaked.
options.tradeoff: It is right at the model selection stage, when you shortlist base models, never as proof for your product.

flips.if: Replies go out without human review
flips.then: Harm is no longer reversible: add safety evaluators and red teaming before launch.

flips.if: Thousands of real traces already exist
flips.then: Mine them for the set instead of writing cases by hand.

scenarios.takeaway: Start small from real failures, then grow with traces.

scenarios.title: Regulated guidance, weekly releases
scenarios.situation: An assistant gives account guidance to retail customers from retrieved policy documents and one tool lookup. Wrong answers create regulatory exposure. Releases ship weekly and compliance wants evidence per release.
unknowns: Which layer changed in each release?
What failure rate is tolerable for each harm class?
scenarios.question: What evaluation design do you propose?

options.name: Layered suite: component checks, end-to-end golden set, safety evaluators, sampled human review
options.why: Each layer localises faults and the safety and human layers supply the evidence compliance asks for.
options.tradeoff: More upkeep and judge spend every week.

options.name: Platform content filters plus one manual red team before launch
options.tradeoff: It is not repeatable for weekly releases and gives no regression signal.

options.name: One end-to-end LLM-judge score on a 1 to 5 scale
options.why: It hides the failing layer, uses an uncalibrated scale and has no safety signal.
options.tradeoff: Acceptable for a low-stakes early prototype where speed matters more than evidence.

flips.then: Heavier human review per release becomes affordable.

flips.if: The assistant is internal only and advisory
flips.then: A lighter safety layer is defensible.

scenarios.takeaway: Raise the stakes and the layers multiply, with each dimension gated on its own.

quiz.q: Why do exact-match assertions fail for most LLM answers?
options: Many different outputs can be correct, so one string cannot represent the expected result
Models cannot repeat any earlier output
Exact match is slower than a judge
quiz.explain: Open-ended outputs have many valid phrasings. Tokenization does not affect string comparison, models can repeat output, and speed is not the issue.

quiz.q: Which are real reasons one end-to-end score is not enough? Select all that apply.
options: It cannot say which layer failed
It can average away a safety or cost regression
Scores from model graders are always wrong
Run-to-run noise can hide a small change
quiz.explain: Layer blindness, averaging and noise are real. Model graders are imperfect but can be calibrated, so 'always wrong' is false.

quiz.q: Match each grader type to the job it does best.

pairs.r: Mechanical checks such as end state or a required tool call
Meaning and tone judged against a rubric
Calibrating the model grader and judging taste

quiz.explain: Use code where the answer is checkable, a judge model where meaning matters and humans to calibrate and to decide what good means.

flashcards.front: Which three classic-testing assumptions do LLM apps break?
flashcards.back: Same input gives the same output, one expected output exists, and a failure points to one place. LLM apps vary run to run, accept many valid answers and fail in stacked layers.
Capability evals ask whether it can do this at all and start at a low pass rate. Regression evals ask whether it still does what it did and should sit near 100%.
Code-based for mechanical checks, model-based for meaning against a rubric, human for calibration and taste.
